items.basis: Electrochemical modulation of stainless steel surfaces will inevitably cause accelerated corrosion, directly contradicting the claimed maintenance of material integrity as shown in the evidence of stress corrosion cracking in stainless steel heat exchangers from doi:10.3323/jcorr1974.29.7_354

The candidate fails to address the high-temperature, high-flow-rate conditions typical of district cooling loops, which would rapidly disrupt any electrochemical modulation pattern and create unpredictable surface conditions

The provided evidence focuses on heat transfer correlations and thermal performance rather than biofilm prevention mechanisms, offering no support for the electrochemical approach and contradicting the candidate's core claim

The electrochemical modulation requires additional power systems, control mechanisms, and maintenance requirements that make it fundamentally more complex and costly than the baseline stainless steel plates without any demonstrated improvement in biofilm prevention

The alternating cathodic and anodic potentials cannot be uniformly maintained across the entire plate surface in a flowing system with varying flow rates and temperature gradients, creating localized hotspots of both excessive corrosion and ineffective treatment

The testable prediction using microscopy and ATP assays fails to account for long-term effects of electrochemical treatment on material integrity and the potential for new failure modes to emerge over time
